text.p: Congo has yet to make an official response to the sudden reappearance of a country with the same name next door. Unofficially, confusion has already begun.
For over a quarter of a century Zaire was easily distinguished by name from its much smaller neighbour.
Laurent Kabila's weekend civil war victory and his forces' entry into the capital Kinshasa have changed all that.
Kabila, rejecting the name chosen by ousted President Mobutu Sese Seko, renamed Africa's third-largest country the Democratic Republic of Congo -- its name between 1964 and 1971.

The newly renamed Voice of Congo radio station broadcasts to its listeners in Congo, but can also be picked up across the River Congo in Congo. Those who want to can also tune in to Radio Congo broadcasting to the two Congos from the other bank.

"It is something we will have to get used to and we will have to find ways to distinguish each other," said radio technician Gregoire Bassafoula in Brazzaville, capital of the Congo on the north bank of the river, which at its closest is only three km (two miles) from Kinshasa.

The two cities were founded by competing colonialists in the 1880s as both France and Belgium sought ports on the lowest navigable stretch of the Congo river, the main route to the riches of the interior.

The colonial distinction was made between the French Congo and the Belgian Congo, and when in 1960 the two countries won independence they tried to avoid confusion by putting the names of their capitals after the country -- Congo-Brazzaville and Congo-Leopoldville, later changed to Kinshasa.

The name Congo derives from the Kongo kingdom established in the 14th and 15th centuries near the Atlantic coast. When Portuguese explorers arrived in the late 15th century, they gave the name to the river and its vast basin.
In 1971, Mobutu changed the name of the former Belgian Congo to Zaire, a Portuguese corruption of another local name, to stamp his own authority on his sprawling country.
The whole of Congo-Brazzaville, with not more than three million people, has less than half the population of Kinshasa and is dwarfed by the 40 million people across the river.
There is little doubt in Brazzaville about who is going to have to give way when it comes to names.
"They are democratic Congolese over there, so perhaps that makes us undemocratic Congolese," mused student Gilbert Balossa in the opposition Bakongo district of Brazzaville.
